fact: A barchart.com author says Wall Street had modelled 45% FY2028 revenue growth before Nvidia's CFO guided to about 70%.
why: It is a superseded estimate from before the guidance; P already has the current market estimate and the guidance, which are what an analyst would weigh for the FY2028 total.

fact: A fool.com author reports that Wall Street expects Nvidia's revenue to grow 91% in FY2027 and 66% in FY2028, a second market reading beside Zacks's 88% and 65.5%.
why: Borderline repeat of Zacks's figures, but 66% applied to the $412 billion FY2027 base P already has gives about $684 billion, a market reference closer to the rung 2 floor than Zacks's $671.95 billion (still rung 3).

fact: Trefis says the roughly 70% FY2028 outlook is the first time Nvidia's management has guided a full year ahead.
why: Marginally: it tells an analyst there is no record of how such year-ahead guidance turns out, and P's answer rests on that guidance with little room above the rung 2 floor; it does not change the figure.

fact: Keithen Drury (fool.com) judges that Nvidia's real growth next year is likely higher than management's 70% expectation.
why: A view that growth beats the outlook would put the FY2028 total above the roughly $700 billion P relies on, towards rung 1, though it gives no number.

fact: Trefis describes management's roughly 70% FY2028 growth outlook as preliminary.
why: Marginally: an outlook called preliminary is less firm, and P's answer rests on it with little room above the rung 2 floor; it does not change the figure.

fact: Nvidia says its share of the five largest cloud providers' information-technology capital spending rose from 11% in 2023 Q1 and projects it to reach 44% by 2027.
why: Set beside the spending forecasts P already has (e57 and the spending themes), a company-projected 44% share by 2027 is a way to size Nvidia's revenue from its largest customers in the FY2028 window.

fact: Nvidia's CFO called memory pricing extreme, said together with her expectation that supply stays a bottleneck through FY2028.
why: P already has the memory shortage and price surge from an author and from Micron and the bottleneck from management; the CFO's wording adds no figure for the revenue total.

fact: Nvidia's CEO said on the earnings call that AI agents use 15 to 100 times as much compute as work guided by a person.
why: It is general demand colour with no FY2028 size; Q already has management saying demand far exceeds what supply allows, and supply is what limits growth.

fact: A fool.com author reports that demand for Micron's memory chips far outpaces supply, causing sharply higher memory prices and global supply constraints.
why: Q already has Nvidia's own CFO calling memory pricing extreme and expecting the supply bottleneck through FY2028, so this outside description of the same shortage adds nothing to weigh.

fact: Nvidia's CEO said most AI had just become agentic and predicted that every company will run many AI agents.
why: It is general demand colour with no amount or date, and Q already has the stronger statement that demand far exceeds the supply-limited outlook.

fact: Nvidia said it is working to increase supply to meet customer demand.
why: It concerns the limiting factor but gives no amount or timing, and the outlook Q already has (supply a bottleneck through FY2028) is the same management's view of where that effort leads.

fact: A fool.com author calculated that at $227.38 Nvidia's shares traded at about 15 times expected FY2028 earnings.
why: A share-price multiple on expected earnings says nothing about how much revenue grows.

fact: The CEO's doubling remark, made in September 2026, refers to the number of chips Nvidia sells (chip volume) in calendar 2027.
why: Q's only version says the measure and year are unspecified; twice as many chips in calendar 2027, which covers most of FY2028, would at steady prices mean growth far above the 70% outlook, so an analyst would weigh it against the guidance.

fact: Einride expects its vehicle footprint to reach 1,500 to 2,000 vehicles by 2028.
why: A truck operator's fleet plan carries no stated link to, or size of, Nvidia's revenue.

fact: Einride said about 80% of the customer demand on its platform is suitable for automation in the medium term.
why: It describes another company's customers and says nothing that sizes Nvidia's revenue growth.

fact: Ramez Naam said on 4 August 2026 that Nvidia's CUDA moat is broken in 2026 and 2027.
why: Marginally: it is an unsized outside opinion, but it says Nvidia's software lock-in fails in the very period FY2028 covers, a demand risk an analyst would note even with supply as the nearer limit.

fact: Dave Blundin judged that CUDA is already dead as an inference-time moat and short-lived as a training-time moat, and estimated that 90-95% of AI workload is moving to inference.
why: Marginally: it is an unsized outside opinion, but together the two claims say most future workload sits where Nvidia's lock-in is gone, a competitive risk an analyst would note for FY2028.

fact: Dave Blundin said he had himself written custom kernels for Fable 5 in recent weeks, work that used to need a team of specialists.
why: It is an anecdote offered in support of the moat claim and gives nothing to size Nvidia's FY2028 growth.

fact: AMD's Helios platform is in production, with first shipments late in 2026 Q3 and a larger ramp in Q4 2026 and 2027.
why: A rival's rack-scale system ramping through 2027 is competition inside the FY2028 window that an analyst would weigh as a risk to Nvidia's demand, though supply is the nearer limit.

fact: Anthropic plans to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD MI450-series GPUs on Helios, the first 1 GW beginning in the first half of 2027.
why: A large AI lab committing gigawatt-scale purchases to a rival from the first half of 2027 is sized demand going elsewhere during FY2028.

fact: Microsoft plans to deploy AMD's Helios platform at scale on Azure.
why: Marginally: a major cloud buyer adopting the rival platform bears on Nvidia's demand, but the plan has no size or date.

fact: AMD expects its Data Center segment revenue to more than double year over year in 2027.
why: Marginally: a rival guiding to more than double in the same year bears on how much of that year's spending Nvidia keeps, though it gives no dollar figure.

fact: Keithen Drury (fool.com) expects Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue to more than double to $115 billion next year, growing faster than Nvidia.
why: Near repeat: Q already has Broadcom's own figure doubling to $230 billion in FY2028, which carries the rival-growth point, and the year-earlier doubling does not help place Nvidia's FY2028 growth.

fact: Micron does not expect the tightness in the memory-chip market to ease before 2028.
why: It is a supplier's own timing for a key input, independent support that supply stays tight through nearly all of FY2028 and so that growth stays capped near the outlook.

fact: Keithen Drury (fool.com) forecasts that Nvidia will generate more revenue per quarter than Apple by 2027.
why: It gives no figure for either company, so it cannot place FY2028 growth on the ladder.

fact: Elon Musk said in September 2026 that SpaceX would use Nvidia chips exclusively going forward.
why: A large buyer saying it will use only Nvidia chips bears on demand in the FY2028 window, especially with its capacity targets, though it is not an order.

fact: Musk said SpaceX would end 2026 with about 2 GW of computing power and aims to end 2027 with closer to 10 GW than 5 GW.
why: Several added gigawatts in calendar 2027 from a buyer said to use only Nvidia chips is sized demand inside FY2028, even if, as P's judge noted, it is an ambition and not confirmed revenue.

fact: A Motley Fool author estimates that 1 GW of computing power costs about $50 billion to $60 billion, of which about $35 billion is Nvidia chips and other components.
why: It converts gigawatts of planned capacity into Nvidia revenue, which an analyst needs to size capacity-denominated plans; it is an author's estimate, not a company figure.

fact: How-To Geek reports that shop prices of Nvidia's RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and RTX 5070 Ti have risen to about $800 and $1,200 from launch prices of $429 and $749.
why: Undated shop prices of two consumer graphics cards, with no volume, give nothing to size Nvidia's total revenue growth.

answers: The two answers do not differ: both are rung 2, both rest on management's roughly 70% outlook (about $700 billion on the $412 billion base), both put the market reference in rung 3 and both treat supply as the cap, and each sits at the very bottom of its rung 2 (P about $700 billion against a $692.1 billion floor, Q 70% against a 70% floor). Listed facts explain two differences in the reasons, neither of which changes an answer: Q's reference cites the 66% Wall Street figure (e59) that P lacks, and P weighs and sets aside the SpaceX capacity target (e287) that Q never saw; P's remark that the lower $406.05 billion base would give about $690 billion comes from the dollar wording, not from a missing fact. Neither stored reason uses the other listed facts (the beat-the-outlook view and the 44% share on Q's side; the chip-count doubling in 2027, the rival wins and Micron's timing on P's side), so I cannot tell from the packet whether any of them would have moved either answer, and Q's four unshown statements could not be checked.
